title: How many things should there be on a list? Why the answer is almost never 10
summary: Jason Cohen argues that "Top 10" is an arbitrary number, and that the right count of items on a list depends on its purpose. He walks through cases (1, 3, 5-7, one per team, a full audit checklist, bankruptcy) and concludes that fewer is usually better.

principles.text: Before making a list, ask what its purpose is and whether the count has a good reason; the answer is almost never 10.
principles.quote: Always Ask: **What is the purpose of this list?**

principles.text: Usually fewer items is better; 10 is arbitrary, a product of having ten fingers.
principles.quote: Usually, fewer is better, and the right answer is almost never "10."

principles.text: One priority ensures it gets done as quickly as possible.
principles.quote: It's reductive to say [only one thing is important](https://longform.asmartbear.com/maximized-decision/), but it also ensures that it gets done, as quickly as possible.

principles.text: If you can't hold the list in your head even when trying hard, it has too many items; around seven is the cap.
principles.quote: If you can't keep it in your head, even when you're trying very hard, it's too many items.

principles.text: A fixed set like an audit's flags can be a good list: finishing 100% gives a checklist, felt progress and a clear state-change.
principles.quote: Getting through 100% of a specific set of things is a powerful statement.

principles.text: When a backlog or inbox is hopelessly large, declare bankruptcy: archive it all and let the important things come back.
principles.quote: Declare "bankruptcy"--whether it's the email inbox or the Jira backlog. Archive it all. The important things will come back.
